title: This Historic North Carolina House Is Called Raleigh's Most Haunted And Sits Inside A City Park
excerpt: Some old houses keep their secrets behind locked doors, but one in Raleigh invites you right in. It has a reputation as the most haunted house in the city,
content:
Some old houses keep their secrets behind locked doors, but one in Raleigh invites you right in. It has a reputation as the most haunted house in the city, and a local ghost group even leads free tours through it before Halloween.

The same grounds also hold the tiny home where a future U.S. president was born. Keep reading to learn the story, the legends, and the practical tips you need before you go.

A Haunted Address in the Heart of Raleigh

Ghost stories usually come with creaky country roads, but this one comes with city parking. Mordecai Historic Park sits at 1 Mimosa St, Raleigh, NC 27604, just a short trip from downtown Raleigh.

The park is run by the City of Raleigh, which has kept local history alive through its buildings, exhibits, and displays. It sits close to the Oakwood neighborhood, making it an easy stop for anyone already exploring that part of town.

At the center stands the Mordecai house, a historic home with roots in the mid-1800s and earlier. Around it, a small cluster of historic buildings forms a compact campus of the past.

Don’t expect a sprawling theme park of old homes. The grounds hold only a few structures, yet each one carries a lot of historical weight.

The park has earned a 4.7-star average from nearly 600 Google users, which says plenty about how well that small footprint delivers.

So how did one quiet house earn the title of Raleigh’s most haunted? The answer starts with a ghost tour and a healthy dose of skepticism.

Raleigh’s Most Haunted Reputation

Every October, the house gets a very special kind of guest list. The weekend before Halloween, the Ghost Guild hosts a ghost tour of the property, and it costs nothing to join.

The evening begins in the Visitor Center across the street with a slideshow presentation. From there, groups head into the birthplace of Andrew Johnson, the chapel, and finally the Mordecai house itself.

Here is the twist that makes the tour fun. The guides work hard to explain that most of their findings, mainly sound recordings, have ordinary explanations.

A dark shape crossing a camera lens, for example, was likely a spider or insect.

Still, they leave the final call to you. Believers and skeptics can walk out with very different opinions, and that is part of the charm.

Local lore also mentions a ghostly older woman said to linger around the house. Plenty of people leave without spotting her, so no promises on that front.

Spooky or not, the house has a far longer and more grounded story worth hearing.

Birthplace of a President

Presidents rarely come from places this modest. Tucked on the grounds is the small, humble house where Andrew Johnson, the 17th President of the United States, was born.

The building was not always here. Like several structures in the park, it was moved from its original location and placed on the grounds to preserve it.

That relocation story surprises many first-timers. It also explains why the park feels like a carefully gathered collection rather than a single estate frozen in time.

The birth home is a highlight for history fans and a frequent stop on guided tours. Its size alone makes a point about how far a person can travel from where life begins.

It is also one of the stops on the October ghost tour, so the little house pulls double duty. Few presidential landmarks can claim that.

Next door, a different kind of building tells a gentler story.

The Chapel and Its Neighbors

Small buildings can hold big moments. The park’s little chapel is a popular choice for small weddings, giving couples a historic backdrop without a giant crowd.

It sits among the other historic buildings that make up the grounds. Several of them were brought here from elsewhere to protect them from being lost.

Not every door opens on every visit, though. Some buildings may be closed for safety reasons, and a few have been converted to storage spaces.

That can be a mild letdown for curious explorers. The upside is that the exteriors still tell a story, and the grounds are pleasant to stroll between stops.

History is also still being uncovered here. Archaeologists have worked new sites on the property, and gardeners have turned up old dishes while tending the soil.

For a deeper look inside, a guided tour is the way to go.

Guides Who Love the Past

A good guide can turn dusty rooms into living stories, and the educators here have a strong track record. Guided tours are among the most talked-about parts of a visit.

The staff are known for deep knowledge and real passion. Guides often share fresh discoveries, such as dishes found by gardeners that same morning.

Tours of the house cover the estate and its artifacts, which are well preserved. Many pieces inside are original.

The tours also give serious attention to the enslaved people who worked the plantation. That focus offers a fuller and more honest picture of the property’s past.

Regular tours have cost about $10 per person, a modest price for a detailed walk through time. School and adult groups can arrange visits too.

Quieter days can mean a more personal tour, so timing matters. And if walking isn’t enough, there is a ride waiting out front.

Riding the Historic Raleigh Trolley

Traffic is no fun, but a trolley full of history is a different story. The Historic Raleigh Trolley Tour starts and ends on Mimosa Street at the park.

The ride lasts about an hour and rolls through the city with narration about Raleigh since its creation. It is a relaxed way to see the capital without battling the roads yourself.

After the ride, the experience continues on foot. A walking tour takes guests through some of the houses on the Mordecai property.

The ticket price is small for what it includes. That combination of city sightseeing and estate history makes the trolley a favorite add-on.

Parking along Mimosa Street is adequate for trolley riders. That makes arriving a little less stressful.

Once the wheels stop, the gardens are a fine place to slow down.

Gardens, Grounds, and Who Will Enjoy Them

Not every visit needs a ticket. The outdoor grounds are free to walk, and the area stays calm even with a busy city around it.

Behind the kitchen lies a garden filled with flowers and plants, often described as a colonial garden. It is especially lovely in summer.

Bring bug spray in warmer months. Mosquitoes enjoy the garden just as much as people do.

The grounds are well maintained and make a popular spot for family photos. Birds are frequent residents, adding life to spring outings.

History buffs and couples tend to get the most out of the park. Some families find it kid-friendly, while younger children who are not into history may lose interest quickly.

Clean restrooms are a welcome bonus. Now for the details that help plan the day.

Planning Your Visit and a Gentle Verdict

Timing is everything, even for haunted houses. The park is open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 AM to 4 PM and Sunday from 1 PM to 4 PM.

It is closed on Mondays. Plan around that before driving over.

Tours begin at the Visitor Center across the street. Parking is plentiful, and the park’s location near downtown makes it easy to reach.

Set aside about two to three hours to see everything at a comfortable pace. A shorter stroll works too if you just want the grounds.

For the free ghost tour, watch for the weekend before Halloween. The City of Raleigh website shares current details.

So is it truly haunted? That stays up to you.

What is certain is a compact park packed with real history, thoughtful guides, and one president’s first home, all in a single afternoon.
